chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Is an Inflation Regime?

lessons.title: Inflation Regimes vs. Headline Inflation: A Framework

children.text: Every financial news channel will tell you India's retail inflation came in at 5.2% this month. That number is real, but on its own it tells you almost nothing about what kind of inflation you are actually dealing with. A 5.2% print driven by a spike in tomato and onion prices behaves nothing like a 5.2% print driven by a credit boom pushing up wages across every sector of the economy. Same headline number, two completely different
, and two completely different consequences for your portfolio and for what the RBI does next.

body.text: The headline inflation number tells you how fast prices are rising. The inflation regime tells you why prices are rising, and why is what actually moves interest rates, currencies and stock markets.

Regime literacy is not an academic exercise. The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee, foreign investors deciding whether to hold Indian government bonds, and you deciding whether to sit in gold, equities or fixed deposits are all making decisions based on the type of inflation in play, not just its level.

children.text: Headline Inflation: What the Number Actually Measures

markDefs.definition: The all-India CPI reading that blends rural and urban price data. This is the figure the RBI targets, distinct from state-specific indices or CPI-Industrial Worker.

children.text: Headline inflation in India is read off the

, published every month by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MOSPI). It tracks the price of a fixed basket of goods and services that a typical Indian household consumes, weighted so that the categories eating up the biggest share of a household budget move the index the most. Food and beverages alone carry close to 46% of the weight in the
basket, which is why one bad monsoon or a vegetable price shock can move the headline number more than a year of steady wage growth ever could.
The Regime: What Is Actually Driving the Number

An inflation regime is the underlying economic mechanism causing prices to rise, not the number itself. The same 6% CPI print can come from a supply shock (a bad crop, a war disrupting oil shipments), from demand outrunning supply (too much credit and spending chasing too few goods), or from a monetary regime where money supply itself is expanding faster than the economy can absorb it. A later chapter in this course walks through each of these three engines in detail, using Weimar Germany and 1970s America as the textbook cases. For now, hold onto the simpler point: you cannot read a CPI print correctly until you know which of these forces is sitting behind it.

markDefs.definition: The RBI's operating framework since 2016, under which the Monetary Policy Committee targets CPI inflation at 4%, with a tolerance band of 2% to 6%.

children.text: India runs two separate inflation gauges side by side, and mixing them up is a rookie mistake. CPI measures what households actually pay at the retail level and has been the RBI's official target since the

was written into the RBI Act in 2016. The Wholesale Price Index (WPI), published separately by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, measures prices at the wholesale or factory-gate level and excludes services altogether. Before 2016, WPI was the number policymakers watched most closely; today it is a secondary read, useful mainly for spotting cost pressure before it reaches the retail shelf.
Within CPI itself, economists strip out food and fuel prices to get

, the reading with the most volatile, weather-and-geopolitics-driven components removed. Core inflation moves slower and tells you more about the underlying demand regime; headline CPI moves faster and tells you more about supply shocks. Reading both together, not just the headline print that financial television leads with, is the first skill this course wants you to build.

children.text: This distinction shows up on your trading terminal in real time. A hotter-than-expected CPI print typically knocks the Nifty down in the first hour of trade, as traders re-price the odds of an RBI rate hike. That move often partially reverses once analysts work out whether the surprise came from food prices or from broad-based demand. If you only watch the headline number, you get whipsawed. If you can tell within a day whether you are looking at a supply shock or a demand regime, you know whether that dip is a one-print wonder or the start of a longer repricing.

body.title: Reading a Real Print
body.scenario: Through the months following India's March 2020 COVID lockdown, CPI inflation kept running above the RBI's 6% upper tolerance band even as GDP was about to contract by nearly 24% in the June quarter. Petrol pumps had fuel and factories had raw material stockpiles, but the perishable food supply chain broke down: trucks could not move and mandis shut intermittently, so vegetable prices spiked even as overall demand in the economy was collapsing.
body.prompt: Is this a demand-driven regime or a supply-driven regime? What would you expect the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee to do here, cut rates further to support a collapsing economy, or hold/hike to fight above-target inflation, and why does this combination make the call unusually hard?
body.modelAnswer: This is a supply-side, cost-push shock layered on top of collapsing demand, closer to a mild stagflation than a demand-driven regime. Textbook inflation-fighting would call for higher rates, but the MPC judged, correctly, that a supply disruption in perishables would fade on its own once logistics normalised, while cutting rates further would do nothing to fix a broken vegetable supply chain. The RBI held its policy rate through most of 2020 despite CPI running above the 6% upper tolerance band for several months, explicitly citing the transitory, supply-driven nature of the spike. This is the clearest real-world case of why asking whether a regime is transitory or persistent matters more than reacting to the headline print.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Onion and tomato prices spike 40% after unseasonal rains damage crops in Maharashtra and Karnataka, pushing headline CPI to 6.5%. Core CPI (ex food and fuel), however, stays flat at 4.1%. What is most likely happening?
options: Broad demand-pull inflation across the economy
A supply shock concentrated in a volatile CPI component
Monetary inflation from excess money supply growth
body.explanation: When headline CPI jumps but core CPI barely moves, the spike is almost always sitting in a narrow, volatile component like food or fuel rather than reflecting broad-based demand. A structural or monetary regime would typically show up across core categories too, not just in one seasonal crop.

points: Headline CPI tells you how fast prices moved this month; the inflation regime tells you why, and why is what actually drives RBI policy and asset prices.
India runs two separate gauges: CPI (the RBI's actual target since the 2016 FIT framework) and WPI (a wholesale, services-excluded read). Do not treat them as interchangeable.
Core CPI, headline CPI stripped of food and fuel, is the fastest way to tell a narrow supply shock apart from a broad demand or monetary regime.
The RBI's own target is a 4% midpoint with a 2% to 6% tolerance band; one month outside that band is not automatically a regime change.
The next few chapters build the full toolkit: the three engines behind any inflation regime, then how each has actually played out across history in global and Indian markets.
